questions.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=3.$ Given that the point $P(2,3,9)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=6x-y$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(2,3,9)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,3) & =6(2)-(3)=9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,0,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+4y+x$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,0,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)} & =(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+4(0)+(-2) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)}(y-0) \\ z-8 & =-4(y-0) \\ z & =-4y+8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,0,8)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-4y+8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(0.5,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡((0.5)(2))+\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =4(y-2) \\ z & =4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0.5,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0.5 \\ z=4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}

{\begin{aligned}y=2 \\ z=-2x+\pi \end{aligned}

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0,1,2)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)} & =(0)^{2}+(1)^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(0,1)}(x-0) \\ z-2 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(2,-3,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=6(x-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,-3).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,-3) & =6(2-1)=6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,-3) & ={f}_{x}(2,-3)(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6(x-2) \\ z-3 & =6x-12 \\ z & =6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-3 \\ z=6x-9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=-3,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=6x-9$ (or $6x-z-9=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨6,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨6,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-6\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-6⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-6⟩=⟨1,0,6⟩$ is also parallel to it.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,1) & ={e}^{1-1}+2(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-1) \\  & =1+4 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,1) & ={f}_{x}(2,1)(x-2) \\ z-4 & =5(x-2) \\ z & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,1,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=5x-6$ (or $5x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨5,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨5,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-5\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-5⟩\end{aligned}

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-5⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-5⟩=⟨1,0,5⟩$ is also parallel to it.

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,-6,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{x(y+x)}}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,-6).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,-6):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,-6) & =\frac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{4} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k \\  & =⟨0,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-1,1⟩.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $(1,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =\pi (-1)+(-1) \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )}(x-1) \\ z-(-1) & =(-\pi -1)(x-1) \\ z+1 & =(-\pi -1)x+\pi +1 \\ z & =-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ has the equation $y=\pi.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\pi,-1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x =  \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{4} \sin{\left(2 x + \dfrac{\pi y}{4} \right)},$ find a tangent vector to $C$ at $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0)+\frac{\pi (1)}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-1 & =\frac{\pi }{4}x \\ z & =\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(0,1,1)$ has the equation $y=1.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

To find a tangent vector, we can find a normal vector to each plane and compute their cross product.

- For the plane $y = 1,$ we write $0x + 1y + 0z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

- For the plane $z = \dfrac{\pi}{4} x +1,$ we write $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} x + 0y + 1z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = \left\langle -\dfrac{\pi}4,0,1 \right\rangle.$

Computing the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-\frac{\pi }{4},0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\pi /4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we've found a tangent vector, and this could be our final answer. However, just to make our answer a little nicer, we can multiply the vector by $4$ to yield a simpler, parallel vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)=4\,i+\pi \,k\end{aligned}
$$
